intro: Most people in Brighton and Hove start thinking seriously about a wet room when an ageing bathroom becomes a daily frustration — whether that's a cramped shower cubicle that's seen better days, a family member with reduced mobility who needs safer bathing access, or simply the desire to make the most of a compact bathroom in a terraced house. Wet rooms have grown hugely popular across the city over the past decade, and for good reason: they're space-efficient, easier to clean, and add genuine value to a home. Done well by an experienced installer, a wet room transforms one of the most-used rooms in your house into something that's both practical and genuinely impressive.
localContext: Brighton and Hove's housing stock is one of the most varied in the South East, and it has a real bearing on wet room installation. The city's large number of Victorian terraced and semi-detached properties — particularly in areas like Hanover, Kemptown, and Preston Park — often have narrow, awkward bathrooms on upper floors with suspended timber floors underneath. This matters because timber floors require careful waterproofing and may need structural reinforcement before a wet room former can be properly installed. Post-war properties, common in Whitehawk, Moulsecoomb, and Portslade, often have solid concrete floors which are generally more straightforward to work with. Newer apartments and modern builds in the city centre and marina area typically have the floor construction already suited to wet room conversions. Brighton and Hove is also a hard water area, supplied through the Thames Water and Affinity Water zones, meaning limescale build-up on screens, drains, and fixtures is a real consideration. Experienced local installers will recommend appropriate sealants, drain covers, and fixtures designed to cope with hard water and advise on water softener options.
serviceDetail: A professional wet room installation in Brighton and Hove typically follows a clear sequence of stages, and understanding what's involved helps you know what you're paying for. The process starts with a survey, where the installer assesses your floor construction, drainage options, existing plumbing runs, and the structural condition of the room. This is particularly important in older Brighton and Hove properties where the original plumbing may be in poor condition or the joists need reinforcing. Once the survey is complete and the design agreed, the existing bathroom is stripped out completely — sanitaryware, floor coverings, wall tiles, and in many cases, the original floor screed or boarding. The new drainage channel or point drain is then positioned and connected into your existing waste system, which in some Brighton and Hove terraces means routing through floor voids or boxing around pipes. Tanking — the process of applying a continuous waterproof membrane across every surface — is the most critical stage and should never be rushed. This is followed by laying the sloped former or screed to ensure water flows correctly to the drain, then tiling the walls and floor, fitting the shower valve and head, installing any screen or glass panel, and finally connecting sanitaryware and making good around the room. The whole project typically takes five to eight days depending on complexity.
pricing: Wet room installation in Brighton and Hove generally ranges from £6,000 to £12,000 for a full conversion, though the final figure depends on several factors. A straightforward conversion in a modern property with a concrete floor and simple plumbing access sits towards the lower end. Older Victorian terraces with timber floors, complex pipework routes, or rooms requiring structural work will push costs higher. The specification you choose makes a significant difference too — luxury tiles, bespoke glass screens, thermostatic valves, and premium drainage systems can all add substantially to the total. Brighton and Hove labour rates are broadly in line with wider South East pricing, so budget accordingly and treat any quote significantly below £5,500 with caution.
whyLocal: Hiring a Brighton and Hove-based installer rather than a national firm or someone travelling from outside the area genuinely matters for a project like this. Local tradespeople understand the specific quirks of the city's housing stock — they've worked in dozens of Victorian terraces in Hanover and post-war semis in Portslade and know what to expect when the floor comes up. They're also familiar with local building control requirements and have established relationships with nearby tile suppliers and bathroom showrooms, which can save time and reduce delays. Perhaps most importantly, they're reachable if anything needs attention after the job is done.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an upstairs bathroom in a Victorian terrace in Brighton?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires careful preparation. Victorian terraces typically have suspended timber floors upstairs, which need to be assessed for strength and then properly tanked with a specialist membrane system. An experienced Brighton and Hove installer will have done this many times and will know whether your joists need reinforcing before work begins. It adds some complexity but is entirely achievable.

faqs.q: Will hard water in Brighton and Hove cause problems with a wet room?
faqs.a: Hard water does mean limescale will build up on your drain cover, shower head, and any glass screen more quickly than in softer water areas. The best approach is to choose fixtures designed to resist scaling, use a squeegee on glass after each shower, and descale regularly. Some Brighton and Hove homeowners also install an inline water softener or scale inhibitor as part of the project, which your installer can advise on.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation typically take in Brighton and Hove?
faqs.a: Most wet room conversions in Brighton and Hove take between five and eight working days from strip-out to completion. More complex projects — particularly in older properties with awkward floor construction or extensive tiling — can take up to ten days. Your installer should give you a realistic programme before work starts so you can plan around being without a bathroom.

faqs.q: Does a wet room add value to a Brighton and Hove property?
faqs.a: Generally yes, particularly in Brighton and Hove's competitive property market where well-presented bathrooms make a strong impression on buyers. A professionally installed wet room with quality finishes typically adds value and improves saleability. The caveat is that it needs to be properly done — poor waterproofing or cheap finishes can have the opposite effect, so investing in a reputable local installer is worthwhile.

localParagraph: Brighton and Hove presents a uniquely varied landscape for wet room installation, with its mixed housing stock ranging from grand Regency terraces in Kemp Town and Hove's Brunswick Square to Victorian bay-fronted semis, Edwardian conversions, and post-war properties further inland towards Hollingbury and Whitehawk. This diversity means that no two installations are identical — floor joist depths, existing pipework configurations, and bathroom footprints all vary considerably depending on the era and style of the property. Water hardness in Brighton and Hove sits in a mixed range, drawing from both chalk aquifers and blended supply sources, which means experienced installers should account for potential limescale build-up around drainage channels, linear drains, and thermostatic fittings when specifying materials and sealants. Selecting slip-resistant, fully tanked wet room systems designed to handle moderate to hard water conditions will extend the lifespan of the installation significantly. Working with a contractor familiar with the local property types across areas like Seven Dials, Preston Park, and Portslade ensures the project is approached with the practical understanding these varied homes genuinely require.
